title: We cannot but speak (Acts 4:13–20)
hook: ordinary uneducated men astonish the council

segments.voice: Yesterday, the man at the Beautiful gate, and silver and gold I have none. Your line was what I have I give. Who did you really look at? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Picture a nervous witness in a courtroom: no law degree, no fancy words, just someone who saw what happened. The lawyers circle. And then, sometimes, the plainest witness in the room is the hardest one to shake, because they're not arguing a theory. They're just telling what they saw. After the healing at the gate, Peter and John spent the night in custody. Now they're standing before the council, the leading priests and elders, the most educated men in Jerusalem. And next to them stands the man who used to beg at the gate.
screen: `THE PLAINEST WITNESS.` → `A NIGHT IN CUSTODY.` → `THE HEALED MAN STANDS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: The council asks, by what power, by what name, have you done this? Peter answers: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. And then Luke describes the council's reaction. They saw the boldness of Peter and John, and realized they were unlettered, ordinary men, and they were amazed, and they recognized that these two had been with Jesus. Two words in the Greek are worth knowing. Agrammatoi: unlettered, not trained in the schools of the law. And idiōtai: ordinary people, private persons, not officials. English later got the word idiot from it, but here it just means laymen. The Douay calls their courage constancy. The Greek is parrēsia, freedom of speech, the boldness to say everything plainly. And the council can't say much back, Luke notes, because the healed man is standing right there. So they order the two to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus at all. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you judge. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." Notice, it's not stubbornness, and it isn't a debating point. They simply can't un-see what they saw. It's the word from four days ago, witness, under pressure. And the reason given for their boldness isn't schooling. It's that they had been with Jesus. Catholics see the same pattern in many saints with little education, like Catherine of Siena, who learned to write late, and was later named a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `BY WHAT NAME?` · `UNLETTERED, ORDINARY MEN.` · `THEY HAD BEEN WITH JESUS.` · `WHAT WE HAVE SEEN AND HEARD.` · then, large: `WE CANNOT BUT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember what you've seen. Sit and breathe. Let your mind go back to one thing you've witnessed yourself that you can't un-see: an act of kindness that stopped you, a recovery, a forgiveness, a moment in prayer, something beautiful. Not something you read. Something you saw or heard. Let the details come back. Then think of who might need to hear about it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, and hold the line, we cannot but speak. If you don't, just hold the memory. The bell holds the time.
We cannot but speak. Peter and John before the council: they can't stay silent about what they've seen and heard. Today's word.
Your line: we cannot but speak. Today, tell someone about that thing you saw, plainly, without dressing it up. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics read the Acts of the Apostles at Mass through the Easter season, and the Church honors Catherine of Siena, a Doctor of the Church with little formal schooling, on April 29.

original.note: Greek: boldness, frankness, saying everything (Acts 4:13). The Douay has constancy.

trapdoor: what you thought: brave men defying authority.
what it means: ordinary people who can't un-see what they saw, and whose boldness comes from having been with Jesus.
what a scholar hears: agrammatoi and idiōtai mean untrained and lay, not illiterate fools; parrēsia, frank speech, becomes a key word in Acts (4:13, 29, 31).

sources.quoted: For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

notes: Acts 4:13 and 4:19 paraphrased (Douay 4:13 has 'illiterate and ignorant men'; not quoted).
Agrammatoi and idiōtai glosses: standard lexicon senses. Confirm.
Catherine of Siena: little formal education, learned to write late in life (traditionally), declared Doctor of the Church in 1970; feast April 29. Confirm.
The council (Sanhedrin) is presented neutrally as the city's leaders; Keeper to confirm the framing is fair.
